newsitem.title: ROMANIA: State bank selloff bill clears Romanian parliament.
newsitem.headline: State bank selloff bill clears Romanian parliament.

text.p: Romania's parliament gave final approval on Friday to a bank privatisation bill, clearing another hurdle for restoring international credits ahead of an International Monetary Fund meeting.

The IMF viewed the legislation and passage of the budget as key steps to renewing the credits it suspended last year after complaining about the former leftist government's overspending. A decision on the loans is to be taken next week in Washington.

"The law straighten things out," Reform Minister Ulm Spineanu told the Chamber of Deputies after it had approved the bill by 218 votes to 32 -- a day after the 1997 budget was passed under accelerated emergency procedures.
The upper house, the Senate, passed the bill earlier in the week at the urging of the centrist coalition government.
The law was approved following two unsuccessful attempts in 1996 to introduce similar legislation under the leftist government voted out of office last November.

It allows state-run banks to turn private by raising capital through share issues or by sales of stocks held by the majority shareholder, the State Ownership Fund (FPS), or through a combination of the two.
Stocks can be aquired by Romanians or foreign individuals and corporate investors, who may pay only cash.
The FPS, brought under government control this week, can retain a "golden share" in banks going private, enabling it to veto decisions like mortgaging assets, mergers or liquidation.
No single stockholder can acquire more than 20 percent of the equity, with the exception of "reputable" international financial and banking institutions.
Mircea Cosea, Reform Minister in the leftist administration defeated last November, said the bill's main drawback was a lack of clarity in protecting domestic investors' interests.
No purchases can be made on the strength of credits from local banks and any share acquisition larger than five percent must be approved by the central bank (BNR).
Banca Romana pentru Dezvoltare, financing investments, would be the first of six state-run banks to go private.

Other candidates are Bancorex, which handles much of Romania's foreign trade, Banca Agricola and Banca Comerciala, specialised in farm and industry lending, Banc Post, operating through post offices and Eximbank, which supports exporters.
There are 40 commercial banks in Romania and the sector is one of the fastest growing since the 1989 fall of communism.

No bank has so far been declared bankrupt in Romania, though the central bank has announced that two debt-ridden private banks -- Dacia Felix and Credit Bank -- are to lose their banking licences after unsuccessful rescue packages.
The government plans to revise laws to enhance bank supervision and set rules for liquidation which are different from those applying to commercial companies.
Economists say the case-by-case approach might slow down sell-offs but say it will take account of each bank's nature.
